tools.title: The most valuable nomination of all time?
tools.summary_raw: On Still Counting EP11, we talked about Jon Ossoff and the bright but uncertain future for Democrats.
tools.content_text: The view from the Lincoln Memorial on Nov. 7. Nate Silver. Ironically, because Washington is so close to New York, I don’t really see much of the city. It’s not like going to LA where, even on a work trip, I’ll plan some excursions — it’s pretty much in and out. But I did get to spend some time on Saturday, on a crisp afternoon, walking and running along the National Mall. The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool looks great, by the way; the White House does not . I was also in DC for the 2008 presidential election, and of course there were lots of celebrations even in a famously buttoned-up town. Midterms aren’t like that and don’t trigger the same outpouring of emotions (except maybe, this year, in Austin ). And that’s fairly rational, I suppose. Republicans have nothing at all to celebrate, except maybe Florida and some comparative overperformance in New England . But for Democrats, the job is only half-done. Even with large majorities in the House and Senate, Congress will serve as less of a check on a president’s power when he exercises most of his authority through executive actions anyway — and the powers of the executive branch are interpreted liberally by courts. The 2026 midterm will go down in the history books , and the election was played for keeps. Democrats will probably hold the Senate even if they lose the presidential race in two years. But the total and complete repudiation of Trump that Democrats are hoping for will require flipping the White House in 2028, too. So in our Still Counting live show in Washington on Saturday, we talked about what the future holds for Democrats: Audio version here. As always, we’re grateful for any reviews, comments, likes and subscribes. Note that this was taped in front of a live audience. The context You can accuse us of pandering to the crowd, but Galen, Clare, and I conducted a “mini-draft” of Democratic primary candidates. The truth is, it didn’t differ that much from our last pre-midterm draft . But this time, I was lucky enough to draw the first pick and chose who is technically the senior Senator from Georgia, Jon Ossoff. I selected his colleague Raphael Warnock with my second pick, and Gavin Newsom in the third round. (I’m not a fan of the latter exactly, but I’ll grab value when I see it.) At prediction markets, Ossoff is now the frontrunner by some margin, with about a 1-in-4 chance of becoming the nominee — AOC is second — although traders are also not necessarily convinced that he’ll run. Subscribe now There’s perhaps a little bit of a syndrome here of Ossoff having become the consensus #1 overall NBA/NFL pick with a degree of projection involved. I was going to write something about how he hasn’t really “proven” anything, but that’s inherently true for basically any potential presidential nominee. And this is not exactly a “stats vs. scouts” thing. Ossoff won Georgia by 18 points on Tuesday. […]

tools.title: Nov. 10: A Groundbreaking Local News Tool With Roots in Oregon
tools.content_text: A few weeks ago I got an Zoom invite from longtime friend Andrew DeVigal at the University of Oregon about a project he has spent eight years researching and the last several months building. DeVigal was the designer of the original ChicagoTribune.com site we worked on three decades ago (which I wrote about a few weeks ago.) So when DeVigal told me he had a cool project to show me, I showed up on Zoom. His creation: The Oregon Civic Newsstand , which helps Oregonians find the local reporting they can use to take part in civic life. It went live last week. Every day it reads every Oregon news story it can rightfully assess, across all 36 counties, and names what each one does: who decided and who answers for it, how to show up, what is already working. Anyone can browse This Week and This Month. A free membership adds Today and Yesterday, each story’s civic value, and the full assessment behind it. It is a project of the Agora Journalism Center at the University of Oregon School of Journalism and Communication, where DeVigal works. Sponsor Can’t get to every city council and school board meeting? SeeGov follows them for you, lets you search what was said, and helps you turn the best moments into shareable video. Built for small teams with a lot of ground to cover. The site is a culmination of eight years of research in which DeVigal and his team asked Oregonians what they need from local news: seven information needs assessments since 2018, 2,118 survey responses, and listening sessions in communities from Hermiston to the Rogue Valley to Lincoln County. One question kept surfacing, in one form or another: where do we find news we can actually use? Reading all seven reports together, one thing stood out. Residents have jobs to do. Journalism is what they hire to do those jobs. That makes news a utility. People hire news outlets to know what is happening, who should answer for it, and how they can take part. Those jobs became The Eight Dimensions of a Civic Story . “We don’t judge the craft,” DeVigal said. “We describe what a story does for a community.” This is not a checklist for journalists to follow. Not every journalistic piece is a civic story. And hardly any local news story does all eight dimensions at once. Opinion, editorials and columns often set out to persuade, and while many are carefully reported, they fall outside what the Newsstand measures. Same with obits and sports coverage stories. The reading is AI-assisted. The Oregon team designed the rubric, set the gates that decide which stories get assessed, and correct the model by exception. “The principle I work from comes from Audrey Tang ‘s work in Taiwan: technology assists, people decide,” DeVigal said. “The model applies judgment and never authors it. A validity study is underway comparing the system’s civic scores against independent human coders. […]

market.title: AFP builds a new funding model for investigative journalism
market.summary_raw: AFP is known for breaking news. Now, the global agency is testing a philanthropic model to fund deeper, more consequential journalism. At the Asian Media Leaders Summit, AFP's Karl Malakunas shared what it has learned so far.
market.content_text: By Maria Lisicka With 1,700 journalists in 151 countries, Agence France-Presse documents events around the clock. But Karl Malakunas , its Head of Philanthropic Partnerships, described a different kind of experiment they have under way: “a completely new editorial and funding model for AFP” for in-depth and investigative journalism. Malakunas, an Emmy-nominated and Walkley Award-winning journalist, joined AFP in Hong Kong 25 years ago. “Breaking news is in my veins,” he said. Yet, like a lot of journalists, he always wanted “to scratch that itch” of going deeper. He did so in the Philippines, turning a 700-word article on environmental defenders in Palawan into a 90-minute feature documentary. The film took 10 years and was largely funded by foundations. In March 2025, AFP’s global news director asked him to bring that approach inside the agency. AFP gets about a third of its funding from the French state and two-thirds from its 4,000-plus clients. Philanthropy adds a third stream, focused on the “Future of the planet” and the “Future of societies.” Above all, editorial independence must remain “sacrosanct,” Malakunas said. A global desk for environmental justice The first project is AFP’s Environment and Climate Legal Desk, billed as the world’s first global newsroom unit dedicated to environmental and climate justice. Its specialist reporters will support AFP’s bureaus on cases too complex for busy news teams, such as SLAPP suits (lawsuits designed to silence critics) in the Philippines. Raising the money proved to be the more difficult part. “It’s definitely harder, the fundraising element than the editorial element,” Malakunas said. “We’re not going to sugarcoat that.” AFP bypassed traditional journalism funders to approach environmental foundations, “a long, slow process.” The desk now has a founding editor to build and lead it, and is hiring reporters in Asia, Africa and Latin America. Impact you can document Working with The Gecko Project , which brought the story idea, AFP put its boots on the ground to reveal that an Indonesian mill supplying Asia Symbol, a Chinese maker of “so-called carbon-neutral packaging,” had processed wood from plantations where orangutan habitat had been cleared. Haleon, the British maker of Panadol, then dropped Asia Symbol as a packaging supplier for its China operations. AFP now documents such outcomes. Asked how impact is measured for funders, Malakunas said AFP is building its first impact tracker. Beyond distribution reach, it asks: “Is it cited by civil society? Is it cited by lawmakers? And did it lead to anything?” The results go back to funders. As AFP reaches audiences through its media clients, journalists will log impact themselves. “It’s boots-on-the-ground journalism. That’s the differentiator … And it’s expensive and it’s hard to do.” – Karl Malakunas, Head of Philanthropic Partnerships, AFP Protecting independence AFP published a code of ethics on day one. […]

market.title: Taiwan’s CommonWealth Magazine doubles down on data-driven investigative journalism
market.summary_raw: Is investigative journalism too difficult and expensive? "Definitely yes," said Yi-Shan Chen, Editor-in-Chief of Taiwan's CommonWealth Magazine – but that is not the whole story. She recently explained how an open newsroom culture, unconventional data and AI help to lower the risk of failure.
market.content_text: By Maria Lisicka Despite the challenges and costs of investigative journalism, pursuing it is paramount for news publishers: “The externality is much bigger than its cost,” Chen told participants at WAN-IFRA’s Asian Media Leaders Summit recently in Singapore. Chen cited Reuters Institute research ranking original investigations and on-the-ground reporting as top priorities for news executives in the AI era. “The reality is very simple,” Chen noted. “AI and video have already completely changed how people consume news.” Breakthrough investigative reports, she argued, “send a powerful wake-up call to both society and our subscribers. They remind people the media are here and that we create value that AI can never replace.” No investigative unit, but an investigative culture Chen’s first takeaway was counterintuitive: CommonWealth’s most popular investigations did not come from a dedicated investigative unit. “Every single beat has the potential for deep investigative work,” she pointed out. The key is “an open editorial culture where all journalists can pitch early leads [and] hold honest discussions.” Once committed, the newsroom backs the work with proper, not excessive, resources, ensuring that “when we bet our resources, we deliver something significant.” Reading China through unconventional data As examples, Chen showed two projects built on “unconventional data from China.” First, CommonWealth worked with scholars from Taiwan’s Academia Sinica, using AI to analyse more than 10 years of CCTV footage of Xi Jinping’s face, speech and gait. The finding: Xi looked noticeably thinner at the 2025 military parade, but his health was “actually quite stable for his age.” The second project was personal. “I come from the most dangerous place on earth,” Chen noted. “It’s related to our life.” It began in 2020, when a CommonWealth reporter on holiday in Tainan kept hearing fighter jets scrambling overhead and asked herself: are we going to have a war? The available data was terrible, Chen said: two static PDF images a day from Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense. A team of just three logged every flight path and aircraft type by hand, for a full year. What emerged was striking. The sorties were not aimed at Taiwan at all. Coordinated with the Chinese navy, they pushed southwest towards the South China Sea, a sign, Chen explained, that Beijing’s real goal was to break through the “first island chain” from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines. “It’s not only a Taiwan story,” she concluded. “It’s actually an Asia story.” From three reporters to a live dashboard In 2023, AI took over the mapping and data entry. By 2025, the project had become a fully automatic dashboard tracking Chinese military activity every day, later expanded with Japanese and Philippine data. Then Beijing’s playbook shifted to “grey zone” warfare. The team began tracing China Coast Guard ships day by day, using AI to scale up to more than 1.8 billion lines of ship-tracking data. […]

Sarah wrote about the Local Journalism Initiative in its early days. A...
market.content_text: Canada’s proposed federal budget includes some good news for local journalism . The federal government is extending its journalism tax credit by $501 million, expanding eligibility to audio and audiovisual news organizations, and renewing the Local Journalism Initiative , which supports journalism in underserved communities. Sarah wrote about the Local Journalism Initiative in its early days. A study earlier this year found that reporters paid with LJI funding believed they maintained their roles as watchdogs and wrote balanced stories, though two-thirds of interviewees were concerned about the perception of a conflict of interest. A growing number of journalists say the benefits of government subsidies for journalism outweigh the drawbacks. A recent report in The Tyee suggests government support is essential to the survival of local media in Canada. (The Tyee has received support from the Local Journalism Initiative.) “It’s either this or death, frankly,” LJI program director and Canadian Association of Journalists president Brent Jolly told The Tyee. “It’s not about local news editors getting their marching orders from the Prime Minister’s Office like some conspiracy theorists want you to think. It’s about infrastructure.” Lisa Sygutek , publisher of the Crowsnest Pass Herald in Alberta, credited the LJI with growing the publication from “a 16-page paper to a 24-page paper.” Read more in The Tyee’s look at Canadian local news here .

market.title: Student journalists are reporting more local news for real audiences. Their professors are exhausted.
market.summary_raw: If there’s one big takeaway from the past two decades of local news struggle — the often perilous, occasionally brilliant transition from dominant newspapers to online media — perhaps it’s this: Passion alone isn’t enough. A newspaper newsroom filled with committed editors and brilliant reporters still stares into the same headwinds as its more middling peers....
market.content_text: If there’s one big takeaway from the past two decades of local news struggle — the often perilous, occasionally brilliant transition from dominant newspapers to online media — perhaps it’s this: Passion alone isn’t enough. A newspaper newsroom filled with committed editors and brilliant reporters still stares into the same headwinds as its more middling peers. The devotion of those leading a nonprofit outlet can mean little if revenue can’t keep the doors open. And even when the money is less important — when journalism is somewhat protected from the demands of the market — passion is still a finite resource, and it’s not always renewable. That truism came to mind when I was reading a recent article by Sima Bhowmik of the University of Vermont and Andrea Lorenz of Kent State. It looks at one specific corner of the contemporary news ecosystem: journalism schools that use their students to fill voids in local coverage. J-schools, after all, have faculties full of experience and students who need it. A few decades ago, an early-career journalist might have spent a few years covering city council meetings and school board budgets before moving up the chain to a bigger outlet. That path barely exists these days, and journalism programs know their students need the chance to do real work. What if these reporters-in-training could handle some of the local stories that the city’s daily no longer can? If you happen to live near a college with a journalism program, you’ve probably seen this idea — often called the “teaching hospital” model — in action. Here in the Boston suburbs, many of the stories I read about my town are written by Boston University students . According to UVM’s Center for Community News , where Bhowmik is a post-doc research fellow, there were 282 such efforts as of 2025, producing local news inside 205 colleges and universities. Those numbers were up from 227 programs in 172 colleges the year before — a boom fueled by a surge in philanthropic funding for these partnerships. Bhowmik and Lorentz’s paper — published in Journalism & Mass Communication Educator — is the result of interviews with 118 faculty and staff at 101 of those colleges, and their major takeaway is one that will be familiar to many in local news: They’re exhausted . Participants repeatedly used phrases such as “at capacity,” “don’t have the bandwidth,” “not enough hours of the day,” and “it’s just a lot” to describe the workload. Several described long workdays and exhaustion, with one participant saying the amount of editing “just about kills me every semester.” At many institutions, faculty workload was intensified by staffing shortages, retirements, hiring freezes, and budget cuts. This left faculty with little time to provide the one-on-one coaching necessary to elevate student stories to publishable quality… “What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me.
